idiom_name: use-case functions in one translation unit + opaque context struct and vtable ports
implementation_notes: C has no classes, so the application service is a translation unit whose public header declares one function per use case; the context is an opaque struct pointer holding the ports as a table of function pointers (the C equivalent of a vtable, as Samek's Object-Oriented Programming in C describes), wired once in the composition root. What replaces the classic structure is not a language idiom but explicit convention: an int return code per use case, a begin/commit/rollback pair around the orchestration, and a context parameter on every call. The two-part form (opaque context + function table) is still justified when the surrounding codebase already uses function-pointer tables for its repositories, because the service then cannot be written in a different style than the ports it calls.
pitfalls: There is no RAII: every early return must roll back explicitly, or the connection keeps a half-open transaction (goto-based cleanup is the usual C answer).
A single global context struct turns the 'stateless service' into shared mutable state and breaks concurrent use; keep the context read-only and pass the transaction handle as a parameter.
Function-pointer tables are not type-checked beyond the struct declaration: a mismatched signature compiles and fails at runtime as undefined behaviour.
